Title: Embracing contextual vs. behavioural targeting

URL Source: https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/behavioural-vs-contextual

Published Time: 2021-03-29T13:04:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Behavioural targeting has long been one of the default targeting methods on a marketer’s programmatic campaign checklist. Since the 1990s, the cookie has made tracking in-browser user behaviour a valuable tool for targeting digital ads toward receptive consumers. But with new regulations around the use of cookies, behavioural targeting will need another tactic to supplement—which means it’s time for advertisers to consider using contextual vs. behavioural targeting.

Some browsers are phasing out 3rd-party cookie tracking. This means that behavioural advertising will be more restricted in the coming years. Marketers will need to adjust by embracing new targeting methodologies, like [contextual targeting](https://www.stackadapt.com/contextual-targeting).

To prepare you for these changes, we’ll explain the benefits of both targeting methods, when to use them and how to leverage them for best campaign performance results.

## **Behavioural vs. contextual targeting**

Let’s look at the differences between contextual and behavioural targeting.

Since contextual advertising focuses on what the user is currently seeking on the internet, it offers the opportunity to align with a user’s current frame of mind. This can lead to higher conversion rates with contextual vs. behavioural targeting.

But, this doesn’t mean contextual is the “be all, end all” of programmatic advertising. Both targeting methods interplay and have their place in your overall marketing mix. Therefore, it’s important to understand behavioural as well as contextual targeting, so you can leverage each one effectively to optimize your campaign performance.

### **What is behavioural targeting**

Behavioural targeting, often referred to as audience targeting or demographic targeting, aims to ensure that an ad is relevant to the user visiting a page. This is done by serving ads based on a user’s web-browsing behaviour. User data is collected from various sources using a user identifier like a tracking pixel or cookie.

Data collected from pixels is stored in a data management platform (DMP) or a programmatic advertising [demand-side platform](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/demand-side-platform) (DSP). Some of the data will include information about page visits, ad clicks, or time spent viewing particular content.

The resulting data is analyzed and used to create targetable audiences that represent specific shopping and search habits. For example, if a user clicked on ads for espresso makers, it can be established that the user has an interest in this product.

Behavioural targeting relies on the user’s past actions to understand the kind of purchase they are likely to make. If a user performs an action, online or offline, they will enter a user pool or audience list. A cookie or online identifier is then applied to each user in this group. Once an identifier is linked to a user, it can track them as they browse the internet and serve them ads based on their behaviour.

The benefit of behavioural targeting is ensuring your ad is relevant to the user viewing it. This targeting method has been widely used in online advertising for over a decade. And as the collection of user data becomes more advanced, so has behavioural targeting capabilities.

One of the primary differences between behavioural vs. contextual targeting is that behavioural targeting is focused on the viewer specifically, and not the content of the page on which the ad appears. Let’s take a look at a brief example.

There are two people living in a home that are using the same computer. One is interested in power tools, while the other is interested in baking. If our baker is the one interested in making an online purchase, seeing power tool ads isn’t appealing to them. In the case of behavioural targeting, they may still see those types of ads based on the behavioural history on that shared device.

In this same scenario contextual advertising would ensure the baker is served ads based on what content they are browsing. If they are browsing recipes on a baking blog, contextual targeting will align with that content.

### **What is contextual advertising**

Rather than targeting ads based on user behaviour, contextual advertising targets ads based on the environment in which the ad appears. This targeting method uses algorithms to target ad placements based on keywords, website content, and other metadata. This way, ads are shown to users based on the content they are consuming at that moment in time.

The main difference between contextual vs. behavioural targeting is that behavioural targeting focuses on ensuring the ad is relevant to the user. Contextual advertising targets based on the context of the content on the page where the advertisement appears.

In this way, contextual advertising essentially targets users while they have a particular frame of mind—based on the context of the page they are viewing. For example, if a user is reading a blog about coffee, they could be served ads for coffee beans or coffee makers since it’s likely that the user is thinking about coffee-related products at that time.

Because contextual targeting displays the right ads to your users at the right time, it also helps businesses preserve their brand image. Ads related to what a user is searching that display in real-time are more likely to be seen as helpful and informative.

## **Contextual advertising** is effective and beneficial

Showing your potential customers what they’re looking for, and when they’re looking for it, is just one feature that makes contextual advertising so effective. This alone is reason enough to embrace this targeting method, but in fact, contextual advertising has other benefits. Here are 4 reasons why contextual targeting is both effective and beneficial:

1.   This targeting tactic allows you to reach users when they are in a receptive frame of mind. When a person is browsing content about a specific topic, it signals their intent at that moment, instead of targeting based on their past actions.
2.   Contextual targeting isn’t constrained by [privacy legislation](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/ccpa-in-effect/). Because it doesn’t collect or use information about users, it protects user privacy. Instead, it leverages the context next to which the ad appears.
3.   If your DSP offers an advanced contextual advertising solution, it will provide an opportunity to target niche contexts. You can choose to target by a general topic or use a collection of phrases for more precise targeting. Instead of targeting “coffee,” you can use input phrases like “organic coffee beans,” “organic coffee,” and “dark beans” to narrow the context even further.
4.   Since c[ontextual advertising campaigns](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/downloads/guide-to-contextual-advertising/) are served programmatically, you can review real-time metrics and optimize your contextual advertising performance. Your DSP should allow you to verify that your ads are served on relevant domains pre- and in-flight. This gives you the ability to revise your selected topics and phrases in real-time to improve the performance of your campaigns.

Since contextual ads reach consumers in the right frame of mind, less money is spent reaching your ideal customer. You may also see above-average conversion rates on contextual campaigns for the same reason. This adds up to an increased return on ad spend (ROAS), and it’s all possible because of the unique way that contextual advertising targets.

## **How contextual advertising works**

We’ve covered the features of contextual vs. behavioural targeting. But how does contextual advertising actually work? Let’s dig into the basic process for [contextual ad placement](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/webinars/how-to-use-contextual-targeting/).

If your DSP offers contextual advertising, the platform will do the heavy lifting of placing your ad on web pages that meet your targeting parameters. Once you have your creative all set to go, you’ll set up your custom contextual strategy.

Here’s an example of how it works: in the campaign setup, identify in context and out of context phrases for your campaign. Then, an algorithm will determine the best ad placements based on a publisher or site’s content using contextual artificial intelligence (AI). With [contextual AI](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/contextual-advertising/), targeting can be expanded further to include relevant phrases related to the context.

results.title: 4 reasons to bake cookieless advertising into your media plan

Title: 4 reasons to bake cookieless advertising into your media plan

URL Source: https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/cookieless-targeting

Published Time: 2022-03-11T16:04:17+00:00

Markdown Content:
Today’s advertising landscape is seeing growing restrictions on 3rd-party data collection, which is spurring increased interest in cookieless targeting. Cookieless advertising (also known as contextual advertising) isn’t constrained by [privacy legislation](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/ccpa-in-effect/) because it doesn’t collect or use information about users. Instead, it leverages the context next to which the ad appears.

Thanks to current technology, contextual is multi-channel and scalable, making it a reliable means for reaching your audience. Plus, it provides advertisers another option for diversifying methodologies and experimenting with new marketing strategies. That’s a targeting method you can sink your teeth into. Read on to learn what cookieless targeting is, how it differs from behavioural targeting, and the benefits of cookieless advertising.

## What is cookieless targeting

Cookieless advertising targets ads based on the environment in which an ad appears. It uses algorithms to target ad placements based on keywords, website content, and other metadata. This way, ads are shown to users based on the content they are consuming at that moment in time. Modern cookieless targeting leverages machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI), which has made this targeting method more effective than ever before.

### Understanding cookies

[​​What are cookies?](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/what-are-cookies) A cookie, also called web cookie, internet cookie, or browser cookie, is a small piece of data sent from a website and stored on the user’s computer by the web browser. This small, unique identifier enables a website to remember a user as well as their actions as they browse.

Cookies are what makes tracking in-browser user behaviour a valuable tool for targeting digital ads toward receptive consumers.Cookieless advertising offers an alternative to this targeting solution.

## Behavioural vs. contextual targeting

Behavioural targeting, often referred to as audience targeting, aims to ensure that an ad is relevant to the user who is visiting a page. This is done by serving ads based on a user’s web-browsing behaviour. User data is collected from various sources, and typically to collect this data you need some sort of user identifier, like a pixel or cookie.

Rather than targeting ads based on user behaviour, [contextual advertising](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/behavioural-vs-contextual) targets ads based on the environment in which the ad appears. The key [difference between contextual and behavioural advertising](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/behavioural-vs-contextual) is that behavioural targeting aims to identify the ideal user based on the attributes they exhibit, while contextual advertising targets users based on the content they are consuming at that time.

For example, behavioural will assume a user likes shoes because they have been identified as a shoe lover, based on their previous web activity. Whereas with [contextual targeting](https://www.stackadapt.com/contextual-targeting), a user has indicated an interest in shoes because they are actually looking at content about shoes at that very moment.

## The benefits of cookieless targeting

Cookieless targeting offers marketers an opportunity to experiment and innovate their targeting strategies. By adding this strategy to their marketing mix now, advertisers can elevate their results.

Here are 4 key benefits of cookieless targeting:

### 1. Cookieless advertising helps you reach users in the right frame of mind

When a person is browsing content about a specific topic, it signals their intent at that moment.For example, if a user is reading a blog about coffee, they are in a receptive frame of mind when it comes to content and ads related to coffee.

With cookieless targeting, that user could be served ads for coffee beans or coffee makers, as it’s likely at that time the user is thinking about coffee-related products. A person’s content consumption signals intent at a specific moment in time, and with cookieless targeting, you can reach them in that moment.

### 2. Cookieless advertising helps you target niche audiences

Contextual advertising also provides the opportunity for marketers to target niche contexts by specifying a topic or a collection of keywords. For example, a marketer who is running a campaign for a mascara product may want to create value alignment between users and the mascara by highlighting that the mascara is vegan.

Cookieless targeting would enable them to indicate keywords related to vegan makeup to precisely target a niche customer profile. This strategy is effective because it ensures your ads are served to consumers who are receptive to the niche attributes of a product or service.

### 3. Cookieless targeting provides real-time metrics

Since contextual advertising campaigns are served programmatically, you can review [real-time metrics](https://supermetrics.com/podcasts/contextual-advertising-ned-dmitrov) and optimize for maximum performance. With the right programmatic platform, you can verify your ads served on relevant domains pre- and in-flight. This gives you the ability to revise your selected topics and keywords in real-time to [improve the performance of your campaigns](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/cookieless-targeting-drive-performance).

Optimizing your campaigns in real-time strengthens your live campaign’s performance which ultimately improves the outcome. And, being able to make in-flight changes means you’re able to make adjustments that will reduce any ad dollar waste.

### 4. Cookieless advertising is brand safe and builds brand affinity

Now more than ever, consumers care about where they shop, and they are increasingly conscious of the environments where brands choose to advertise. Contextual advertising addresses the need for brand safe advertising while also [building brand affinity](https://www.stackadapt.com/resources/blog/brand-affinity), by leveraging content rather than user data to reach the right audience. You’re able to connect with consumers who are receptive to purpose-driven messaging, and looking specifically for brands that align with specific values.

For example, a consumer who is interested in reducing their environmental impact will likely browse online for content that provides insights on sustainable living. With contextual targeting, a brand that is promoting their zero-waste products can target the keyphrase “sustainable lifestyle,” to appear next to content that covers related topics. This strategy ensures that the brand is reaching consumers who will align with the brand’s values.

## Cookieless tactics do not mean a cookieless future

Is the future of advertising really cookieless? No!

There are a number of digital environments where cookies will continue to exist, acting as identifiers for those who engage with the content and web pages. Aside from instances where a user would accept the cookie notice that they are prompted to respond to on web pages, there are many scenarios where a user would willingly provide their information. This could be in a payment portal, or when providing an email address to download content or access additional information.

What _will_ change is the number of digital environments where cookies are accepted and tracked. For example, some browsers like Apple Safari offer options for users to manage cookies and website data. A user now has the option to block all cookies while using that browser. We are moving toward a digital future that is increasingly cookie-limited, but will not be cookieless. That is why cookieless targeting methods are so critical—they keep your digital strategy from crumbling.

## Example of contextual advertising

Cookieless targeting is especially helpful for marketers in sensitive categories, like pharmaceuticals. This is because behavioural targeting for this industry can be considered as too invasive of user privacy, and in some regions it’s prohibited by law.

With a contextual campaign, products and services in sensitive categories can drive awareness by identifying the phrases and keywords that are most appropriate to target. For example, to drive awareness for a drug rehabilitation center, a marketer would target in context phrases like “addiction,” “counselling,” “mental support,” and “recovery.”

Marketers can also identify out of context phrases, eliminating those phrases within the campaign targeting methodology. So an awareness campaign for that same drug rehabilitation center would want to use out of context phrases to avoid placements such as stories about celebrities and gossip sites.

results.markdown:
Title: Google Ads in Europe 2025: Strategies That Actually Drive Conversions

URL Source: https://www.marcom.eu/google-ads-in-europe-2025-strategies-that-actually-drive-conversions

Published Time: 2025-10-31T11:31:29

Markdown Content:
In 2025, competition for digital attention in Europe has reached new heights. Businesses across every industry are investing more heavily in Google Ads than ever before — but not all are seeing meaningful returns. Why? Because most brands still rely on outdated tactics that no longer resonate with today’s European consumers.

If you want to succeed with**Google Ads in Europe 2025**, it’s not just about running campaigns — it’s about crafting the right**conversion strategies**for a diverse and fast-evolving market. In this article, we’ll explore what’s changed, what still works, and which**Google advertising tips**can truly drive conversions across Europe’s complex digital landscape.

## The Evolving European Ad Landscape

The European advertising environment in 2025 is more dynamic — and fragmented — than ever before. Privacy laws such as GDPR continue to shape how advertisers collect and use data, while AI-driven automation has redefined how campaigns are built and optimized.

In addition, Europe is not one homogeneous market. Consumer behavior varies significantly between countries: Germans value trust and detail, the French respond to creativity and style, while Scandinavians prioritize sustainability and minimalism. This diversity means your**Google Ads Europe 2025**strategy must be hyper-localized — both in language and intent.

## Embrace AI and Automation (the Smart Way)

One of the biggest shifts in**Google Ads Europe 2025**is the dominance of automation. Google’s AI now handles everything from bidding and audience targeting to creative testing. But automation doesn’t mean “set it and forget it.” The most successful advertisers use automation strategically.

Here’s how to make AI work for you:

*   **Feed the algorithm with quality data**— accurate conversion tracking, audience signals, and first-party data are essential.
*   **Use Performance Max campaigns**for multi-channel reach, but layer them with strategic audience exclusions and geo-targeting for precision.
*   **Continuously test ad assets**— even automated campaigns perform best when fed new creatives and messaging variations.

The key conversion strategy here is balance: use AI for optimization but rely on human insight for creativity and positioning.

## Prioritize Local Relevance

European users expect ads that feel personal and culturally relevant. A single “one-size-fits-all” campaign won’t perform equally well in Spain, Sweden, and Poland.

To truly**drive conversions**, adapt your ad copy, visuals, and offers to local contexts:

*   **Language localization:**Always use native-level translations — not automated ones.
*   **Cultural tone:**Consider holidays, idioms, and emotional triggers specific to each market.
*   **Currency and pricing:**Display prices in local currency to reduce friction and increase trust.

One of the most overlooked**Google advertising tips**is the importance of contextual localization. An ad written for London should not read the same as one designed for Berlin.

## Optimize for Mobile and Voice Search

By 2025, more than 70% of Google searches in Europe are conducted on mobile devices. In addition, voice search is becoming increasingly popular thanks to widespread smart speaker use and multilingual AI assistants.

This means your**conversion strategies**must account for:

*   **Shorter, conversational keywords**reflecting how people speak, not type.
*   **Fast-loading landing pages**optimized for mobile UX.
*   **Clear, immediate CTAs**that fit smaller screens.

Voice-optimized ad copy — phrased as answers to spoken questions — can also significantly improve engagement in markets like the UK, France, and the Netherlands.

## Refine Your Bidding and Budgeting Strategy

Automation in bidding doesn’t mean losing control. Smart bidding remains one of the most powerful tools for improving conversions, but only when it aligns with your business goals.

In**Google Ads Europe 2025**, advertisers are seeing the best results with:

*   **Target ROAS**for eCommerce — maximizing revenue based on real conversion value.
*   **Target CPA**for lead generation — ensuring cost-efficient acquisitions.
*   **Maximize Conversions with enhanced signals**— ideal for newer campaigns collecting data.

Set realistic goals and allow campaigns time to “learn.” Avoid the common mistake of adjusting bids too frequently before Google’s algorithm stabilizes.

## Create Conversion-Optimized Landing Pages

Even the most perfectly targeted ad will fail if it leads to a poor landing page. Your landing page is the final step in your conversion funnel — and it must be designed to persuade.

Here’s what works in Europe’s 2025 landscape:

*   **Localized content**— language, currency, and testimonials from local customers.
*   **Fast performance**— Europeans are unforgiving with slow load times.
*   **Minimal friction**— simple forms, visible CTAs, and mobile-friendly checkout.
*   **Social proof**— local trust badges, reviews, and media mentions.

Remember, great**conversion strategies**start after the click. Your ad attracts interest; your landing page converts it into action.

## Use Data Responsibly (and Effectively)

Data privacy remains a defining feature of European advertising. With third-party cookies nearly extinct, brands must rely on**first-party data**and privacy-safe audience targeting.

Practical**Google advertising tips**for 2025 include:

*   Implementing**enhanced conversions**for more accurate tracking.
*   Building**custom audiences**using CRM data and website engagement.
*   Leveraging**consent-based remarketing**compliant with GDPR.

When handled transparently, data can still power highly personalized ad experiences — without violating user trust.

## Measure What Truly Matters

Clicks don’t equal conversions. In**Google Ads Europe 2025**, successful marketers measure beyond surface metrics, focusing on business outcomes like:

*   **Sales and lead quality**(not just volume)
*   **Customer lifetime value (LTV)**
*   **Cross-device conversions**

Use Google Analytics 4 (GA4) to track multi-touch journeys across devices and channels. This will help you understand which parts of your campaigns actually drive profitable actions.

## The Future: Personalization Meets Performance

The future of Google advertising in Europe lies in merging personalization with automation. Title: What Is Contextual Targeting? A Guide for Small Businesses

URL Source: https://adwave.com/resources/what-is-contextual-targeting

Published Time: 2026-08-06T10:04:24+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Contextual targeting** matches ads to the content someone is consuming right now, not to a tracked profile. In U.S. advertiser research, it was the **most widely used** targeting method at **49%**, ahead of demographic targeting at **46%**, geo-location at **44%**, and behavioral targeting at **25%**. [^1]

A plumber watching a Saturday morning home renovation show doesn’t need to be retargeted based on last week’s browsing to see a useful ad. If the segment is about a kitchen remodel, a well-matched plumbing offer can show up because the content says, “this viewer is in a home-improvement mindset.”

## A Plain-English Definition for Small Business Owners

A local business owner usually hears “contextual targeting” and thinks it sounds technical. The plain version is simpler, it means your ad is placed beside content that fits the moment, instead of being aimed at a person because of old browsing behavior. [^1]

### The basic idea

If someone is reading about recipes, watching a home repair segment, or listening to a finance podcast, the ad system looks at that environment and decides whether your message fits. That makes **contextual targeting** an **environment-based** approach, while behavioral targeting is an **identity-based** approach that leans on past actions and tracking. [^1]

For a small business, the difference matters because the page, program, or stream can tell you a lot about intent without asking for personal data. A kitchen contractor cares more about whether someone is in a remodeling context than whether they clicked on a cabinet ad two weeks ago.

The old model depended on following people around the web. The newer model looks at what they’re consuming in the moment, which is one reason contextual targeting has stayed relevant as privacy rules tighten and third-party cookies disappear.

> **Practical rule:** if the ad matches the page, program, or episode the person is in right now, you’re in contextual territory.

| Adoption of Major Targeting Methods Among U.S. Advertisers |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Targeting Method | Share of Respondents | Use Often or All the Time |
| Contextual targeting | **49%** | **28%** all the time, **40%** often |
| Demographic targeting | **46%** | Not provided |
| Geo-location | **44%** | Not provided |
| Behavioral targeting | **25%** | Not provided |

The adoption data above shows why this isn’t an edge tactic anymore, it was already mainstream in the U.S. advertiser mix. [^1] If you want a quick glossary-style reminder later, this [contextual targeting glossary](https://adwave.com/glossary) is a useful reference point.

## How Contextual Targeting Works Behind the Scenes

Modern contextual systems work like a librarian who reads the page before deciding which shelf it belongs on. The process starts with a crawler or analyzer, moves through classification, and ends with the ad server using those labels to decide whether your creative should appear. [^3]

### The five-step flow

The first step is signal collection. The system scans the page or environment for clues such as text, metadata, topics, and sometimes images or video captions. From there, it maps those clues into a taxonomy, a structured way of grouping content so the system knows whether it is looking at cooking, sports, finance, or something more specific. [^3]

Then the system looks at meaning. That matters because **contextual targeting is not just keyword matching** anymore. Modern systems can pre-screen pages with machine learning, then apply semantic, sentiment, and emotion analysis to judge whether a placement is relevant and brand-safe. [^2]

A recipe article can mention “heat,” “seasoning,” and “pan,” while a sports highlight can mention “heat” in a different sense. A system that only follows keywords can get confused, but a semantic system reads the surrounding meaning before it serves the ad.

> The ad decision is built from **page-level signals**, not user identity. That is why contextual targeting still works when cookies are restricted or unavailable. [^2][^3]

![Image 1: A diagram outlining the main types of contextual targeting categorized by taxonomy and media format.](https://cdnimg.co/755dca25-e27d-4989-9ee2-33019b5224a7/40d256aa-b1c2-4e26-83b0-0546835b0c86/what-is-contextual-targeting-contextual-targeting.jpg)

The last pass happens before delivery. The system uses those labels as bidder inputs or pre-bid filters, which is why the process fits naturally inside [programmatic advertising guide](https://adwave.com/resources/what-is-programmatic-advertising) workflows. Google’s documentation describes this kind of page analysis and matching as a content-driven process, not a person-driven one, and that is the basic reason contextual advertising still works in privacy-constrained environments. [^3]

## The Main Types of Contextual Targeting You Will Encounter

The phrase “contextual targeting” covers more than one method, and that’s where many buyers get tripped up. Broadly, the stack moves from simple content labels to richer signals, and from web pages to video, audio, and other formats. [^4][^5]

### Taxonomy is getting more granular

On the taxonomy side, the progression starts with **keywords**, then moves into **subtopics**, **intent clusters**, **sentiment tiers**, and **visual analysis**. That matters because a broad label like home repair can include emergency plumbing, weekend DIY, premium remodeling, and unsafe adjacency, and those are not the same buying situations. [^5]

The more precise the taxonomy, the easier it is to keep a campaign close to the right kind of attention. A local roofer probably wants an “urgent repair” context, while a design-build contractor may want renovation and upgrade contexts that signal a longer buying cycle.

![Image 2: A diagram illustrating the six main types of contextual targeting used in digital advertising and marketing strategies.](https://cdnimg.co/755dca25-e27d-4989-9ee2-33019b5224a7/dbd774c3-d273-4f6a-b8c3-b03847302c07/what-is-contextual-targeting-contextual-targeting-types.jpg)

### Format matters too

On the media side, contextual analysis can work across **textual content**, **image and video context**, and **audio transcription**. Other guidance also points to page text, app metadata, video content, audio cues, and even location signals as inputs, which is why the concept now spans web, mobile, video, CTV, audio, and gaming environments. [^4][^5]

That broader reach changes how small businesses should ask questions. Instead of asking only, “What keyword do I want?”, ask, “What content environment do I want my offer attached to, and how narrow should that environment be?” A more granular setup usually gives you better control over brand suitability and relevance.

The practical takeaway is simple. If you’re working with a platform or agency, ask whether they can target by **topic**, **subtopic**, **sentiment**, and **format**, not just by a list of keywords. That’s the difference between a basic match and a useful one.

## Contextual Targeting in TV and Local Advertising with Adwave

A lot of small businesses first run into contextual logic on TV, not on the open web. A home services owner looking at local TV may care less about a browser profile and more about whether the ad shows up in the right viewing environment, around the right program, at the right moment. That is the same basic idea behind what is contextual targeting, just applied to a screen in the living room instead of a page in a browser.

### What that looks like in practice

For video and CTV, contextual analysis can use **program metadata**, **closed captions**, and **transcripts** to match ads to the show and scene. Verve also notes that contextual analysis can use app metadata, video content, audio cues, and location signals, which helps explain why the same matching logic now stretches across multiple screens. [^6]

Contextual targeting selects placements according to the surrounding content. An ad during baseball programming appears in a different context from one in a general social feed.

Adwave fits that workflow by using audience data and viewing patterns to place ads where they are more relevant to local viewers. A small business can enter a website URL, let the AI generate a broadcast-ready spot, and then launch across **100+ premium channels**. It also gives local advertisers a straightforward path from a website to a TV campaign, which matters when you want your offer to match the viewing context without building a production process from scratch.
